title: Three Days in Toronto and a Danish Promise to Make Insulin
dek: In late 1922 August Krogh, whose wife Marie had diabetes, came home from Toronto with permission to make insulin for Scandinavia and set his conditions before any money was spent.

story.founder: August Krogh and Marie Krogh, with Hans Christian Hagedorn and August Kongsted
story.event: Visiting Toronto and starting insulin production in Denmark on non-profit terms
story.summary: In November 1922 the Danish physiologist August Krogh, whose wife Marie had diabetes, visited Toronto and was entrusted by its Insulin Committee with insulin for Scandinavia. Back in Copenhagen he and Hans Christian Hagedorn, funded by the pharmacist August Kongsted, worked unpaid, and the first Danish patient was treated in March 1923. Their Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium became an independent non-profit institution in 1924.
paragraphs: In October and November 1922 the Danish physiologist August Krogh, a Nobel laureate, was touring the United States with his wife Marie, a doctor and researcher. Marie had diabetes; a Danish biographical dictionary dates her illness to 1920, the Nobel historian Jan Lindsten to probably 1921. Her physician in Copenhagen was the diabetes specialist Hans Christian Hagedorn. Insulin had just been purified in Toronto. Lindsten writes that Marie heard of it from the American diabetes doctor Elliott Joslin at a dinner; the Novo Nordisk Foundation says she persuaded him to go.

Krogh's own account, written in 1924, says he soon saw that a Danish supply would matter: American insulin would be slow to come and kept poorly. The task, he admitted, was far from his own research. He wrote to Hagedorn, who agreed to join, and to John Macleod in Toronto, and spent 23 to 25 November there. The Insulin Committee offered him control of insulin in Scandinavia, though he warned that Danish law allowed no patents on medicines, so he could not legally stop rivals. His own absolute condition was that there be no "furious race" with companies to reach the market.

He was home on 12 December. He and Hagedorn chose a private backer over the state, judging the state too slow. They agreed to work unpaid and to sell insulin at a small profit. The pharmacist August Kongsted, owner of Løvens kemiske Fabrik, agreed to pay for the experiments and said he would prefer no profit at all in Scandinavia. On 21 December, extracts made in Hagedorn's private laboratory lowered blood sugar in rabbits. Addressing Danish doctors on 2 January 1923, Krogh warned it could be months, possibly a year, before patients had it.

It took about ten weeks. Lindsten records the first patient treated on 13 March 1923, and Marie was among the first in Denmark to use insulin. By Krogh's account the factory price was soon about a tenth of Britain's. Demand outran the small plant and supplies were rationed, but he wrote that no patient who had started ever went without. In 1924 Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium became an independent non-profit institution, its earnings meant for research and patients; Lindsten notes Krogh soon stepped back from the business to concentrate on science.

quote.text: Even as the unknowing toil, wedded to sense, So let the enlightened toil, sense-freed, but set To bring the world deliverance, and its bliss;
quote.locator: Chapter III, "Karma-Yog, or The Book of Virtue in Work" (verse 25 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: The Gita asks those who work for the world's good to toil as hard as those who work for gain. Krogh, Hagedorn and Kongsted refused the gain, yet still had to run a strained little factory at full stretch, which may be the harder half of the teaching.

reflection: Two things in this story are easy to miss. Krogh settled his conditions before any money was spent: no race, no pay for the founders, a small profit. And standing in front of Copenhagen's doctors, he told them plainly it might take a year.

You will often be asked how soon something will be ready, sometimes by people who badly need it. An honest estimate, even a disappointing one, lets them plan around you, and it spares you on the days when the work goes slower than you wanted. Krogh's caution cost him nothing when insulin came early.
invitation: Think of one date you have given someone this month. If it was the date you hoped for rather than the one you believe, send them a short note today with the honest one.

research_notes: Who prompted the Toronto visit is told differently. Krogh's own 1924 account says he heard about insulin in the press, laboratories and hospitals during his US tour and wrote to Hagedorn and Macleod; it does not mention Marie. Lindsten (Nobel essay, 2001) says Marie learnt of insulin from the diabetologist Joslin at a private dinner and the couple extended their journey; the Novo Nordisk Foundation and Novo Nordisk say Marie persuaded or urged him. The story gives Krogh's account and attributes the Marie versions to their sources. Lindsten spells the doctor 'Eliot P. Joslin'; the story uses the standard spelling Elliott Joslin. The University of Toronto catalogue shows Krogh's letter to Macleod dated 23 October 1922, so the approach to Toronto predates the visit. Onset of Marie's diabetes: Dansk Kvindebiografisk Leksikon says 1920, Lindsten 'probably in 1921'; both are given. Licence: Lindsten calls it a licence to use the Toronto purification protocol; Lex.dk's August Krogh entry speaks of an exclusive right for Scandinavia; Krogh says the Committee 'delegated' the mission to him and that he had no legal means to stop rivals because Danish law allowed no patents on medicines. The story uses Krogh's wording (control entrusted, no legal protection). Company dates: the Novo Nordisk Foundation and Lex.dk date Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium to 1923; Krogh says an agreement of February 1924 separated it from Løvens kemiske Fabrik as an independent non-profit institution; the story uses 1924 for the independent non-profit status. First patient: Lindsten gives 13 March 1923; Krogh and Novo Nordisk say March 1923. 'About ten weeks' is the interval from the 2 January lecture to 13 March. The price comparison (about one tenth of the UK price) and the statement that no patient who had started went without come only from Krogh and are attributed to him. The quoted words 'furious race' are from the English translation by Breuer and Worrall of Krogh's Danish text. The Gita verse is Krishna's teaching that the wise should act as energetically as the attached, but for the world's welfare (lokasangraha); applied here by analogy.
